'''William Craig''' (November 13, 1918<ref name="google">{{cite book|title=Dictionary of Modern American Philosophers|author1=Shook, J.R.|author2=Hull, R.T.|date=2005|volume=1|publisher=Thoemmes Continuum|isbn=9781843710370|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ijpj1tB3Qr0C|page=548|accessdate=2015-04-13}}</ref> – January 13, 2016) was an [[American people|American]] [[Academy#Academic personnel|academic]], logician and [[philosopher]], who taught at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], in [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]], [[California]]. His research interests included [[mathematical logic]], and the [[philosophy of science]],<ref>{{cite web|title=William Craig|url=http://philosophy.berkeley.edu/news/detail/64|publisher=University of Berkeley|accessdate=15 January 2016|archive-date=January 15, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160115172207/http://philosophy.berkeley.edu/news/detail/64|url-status=dead}}</ref> and he is best known for the [[Craig interpolation]] theorem.

==Biography==
William Craig was born in [[Nuremberg]], [[Weimar Republic]], on November 13, 1918. He graduated from [[Harvard University]] with a [[Ph.D.]] in 1951. He married Julia Rebecca Dwight Wilson and had four children: Ruth, [[Walter Craig (mathematician)|Walter]], Sarah, and Deborah. In 1959, he moved to UC Berkeley. He died on January 13, 2016, at the age of 97.

==Achievements==

Craig is particularly remembered in two theorems that bear his name:
* the [[Craig interpolation]] theorem, and
* [[Craig's theorem]], also known as ''Craig's axiomatization theorem'' or ''Craig's reaxiomatization theorem''.
